abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes essential cellular machinery and is contained within mitochondria. This physical containment shapes the genetic dynamics of mtDNA populations in the cell. In plants (and other non-bilaterians), mtDNA colocalisation is essential for recombination, while other cellular priorities may favour mtDNA spacing through the cell. Given possible physical interactions between mtDNA and the inner mitochondrial membrane and its cristae, it is not clear how readily or often this colocalisation may occur. Only limited, indirect evidence exists supporting the capacity for plant mtDNAs to physically colocalise. Here, we survey evidence from recent and new single-cell timelapse microscopy to quantitatively characterise the motion of mtDNA nucleoids inside vegetative plant cells. We combine biophysical arguments with new microscopy data and spatial statistics to demonstrate the subdiffusive but not internally static nature of nucleoids, demonstrating that they are enriched at the termini of elongated mitochondria and well-spaced through the cell but capable of colocalisation. We also describe other modes of physical motion that may impact the genetic dynamics of mtDNA populations, and discuss the implication of this physical behaviour for cytoplasmic genetics.
